facts.fact: Flowerhorns are selectively bred hybrids, mainly from crosses of Central American cichlids.
Flowerhorns do not occur in the wild. Malaysian breeders developed them by crossing cichlids such as the Red Devil, Midas cichlid, Three Spot cichlid and Redheaded cichlid.
The first-generation fish sold today (Hua Luo Han) are said to date from about 1998. Kamfa strains came from crossbreeding in 2000–2001.
Flowerhorns are fertile, unlike many hybrids.
Adults reach 12–16 inches and live about 8–10 years with good care.
This source gives a lifespan of 10–12 years with proper care.
Flowerhorns are highly aggressive and territorial. They have attacked owners during tank cleaning.
Juveniles keep changing colour and pattern until adulthood, so a juvenile's final look is uncertain.
Minimum tank size is 200 L for one adult; 240 L or more is preferred.
Minimum tank size is 55 gallons (ideally about 4 ft × 2 ft). A breeding pair needs at least 125 gallons, and a tank with large tankmates at least 200 gallons.
This source suggests a tank of about 0.8 m × 0.4 m × 0.5 m.
Keep minimal decor and only a little gravel, because the fish moves a lot and can injure itself on objects.
A bare bottom or thin gravel layer is the standard setup.
Flowerhorns dig and uproot live plants.
Use a canister filter that turns over at least 8–10 times the tank volume per hour.
Water parameters: 26–28°C, pH 7.0–7.8, hardness 10–20 dGH, ammonia and nitrite at zero.
Water parameters: 80–89°F, pH 6.5–7.8, hardness 9–20 dGH, efficient filtration with moderate flow.
Ideal pH is 7.5–8 and temperature is 25–30°C.
Change 30–40% of the water weekly.
Change part of the water every 5–7 days.
At every water change, use a dechlorinator that also neutralises chloramines.
Keep the light on 8–12 hours a day.
Base diet: high-protein pellets with 40–50% crude protein, ideally with astaxanthin, spirulina and added vitamins. Supplement with mealworms, small crickets and frozen whole prawns.
Feed adults 2–3 times a day, only as much as they eat within two minutes.
Foods listed include cichlid pellets, bloodworms, krill, crickets, nightcrawlers, earthworms and carotene-enriched supplements for colour.
Do not feed mammal meat such as beef heart.
Flowerhorns are big eaters and are easy to underfeed.
Feed young flowerhorns 3–4 times a day in small pieces, and stop when the fish seems full.
Feed fry several small meals a day; artemia suits young fish. Once the fish is larger, feed twice a day, morning and afternoon.
Overfeeding raises ammonia and does not benefit the fish.
Overfeeding easily causes bloating (sình bụng).
Feeding too much every day is a mistake.
Live food given without precautions can carry parasites and bacteria. Feeder carp often carry disease.
Before feeding them out, wash feeder fish well, soak them in salt to disinfect, and keep them separately for a few days to watch for illness.
Pellets are convenient and hygienic but harder to digest than fresh food. Limit them while the fish has, or has just had, a gut illness, and beware of counterfeit pellets.
Store mosquito larvae (loăng quăng) in the fridge, not the freezer. If kept too long, they can hatch into mosquitoes.
Genetics set a fish's kok potential. Water quality, dietary protein and low stress decide whether the fish reaches it.
If a young fish lacks the gene for a head hump, changing its food will not make the hump grow.
To get a big kok, start by choosing young fish from parents with large heads.
Keep males in separate tanks, or use a glass divider if several share one tank.
Keepers' tip: place a mirror against the tank for 1–2 hours every 1–2 weeks to provoke a rival display; adding a female is an alternative.
Males generally develop more prominent koks. Expect little visible kok growth before 8–12 months.
Stress from vibrations, reflections and disruptive water changes holds back kok growth. Some keepers cover three sides of the tank.
In a 17-week study with two groups of 12 fish, a specialized feed significantly increased growth and kok development compared with a conventional feed.
In that study, the kok of fish on the specialized feed showed more fat under the stratum compactum and a thicker dermis (203.58 μm).
Gensou describes injected koks as a malpractice to avoid. It says products and tricks sold online do less than patience and consistent care.
Chợ Tốt repeats the claim that cholesterol-rich food builds up the kok, but gives no mechanism.
Chợ Tốt also says beef and beef heart make the kok grow fast but are expensive and should only be occasional extras.
Aquariadise reports the belief that flowerhorns bring good luck and feng shui benefits, and that bigger koks mean luckier fish. It presents these as cultural beliefs, not facts.
In a Thai study, fry immersed in methyltestosterone or mesterolone at 125–500 μg/L did not become all male. Mesterolone at 250 μg/L gave about 27% more males than untreated fish.
Common mistakes include keeping flowerhorns with other cichlids, buying before planning the tank and filtration, and expecting fast kok growth.
Flowerhorns are not community fish. Keep them alone or as a breeding pair, and never with invertebrates.
Ich shows as fine white grains on the body and fins, often after temperature swings.
For ich, raise the temperature to 30°C and use a commercial ich remedy.
For ich, raise the temperature to 86°F for three days and use medication.
Hole-in-the-head shows as pits on the head and along the lateral line and is linked to poor water quality. Better water changes and a varied diet clear most early cases.
For bloat, fast the fish 1–2 days and then give high-quality food. Persistent bloat may mean internal parasites, treated with metronidazole.
Prevent disease with a clean tank and filter, a quality diet and washed decor. Quarantine new fish for at least two weeks.
Water that is too cold can cause digestive illness.
Let tap water stand 24 hours so the chlorine gasses off, or run an air pump to speed this up.
Live foods commonly used in Vietnam: cá chép mồi, cá ròng ròng, cá trâm, cá bã trầu, cá lia thia đồng, ốc bươu vàng, loăng quăng, bo bo and tép.
Fresh tép contains carotene, which helps the fish colour up.
In hot climates where room temperature runs 28–32°C (such as Singapore), a chiller may be needed.
Spawning tank: about 82°F, pH about 7.0, with hiding places and a divider with a flat stone. Feed fry baby brine shrimp first, then crushed pellets after a couple of weeks.
